---
title: "Workspace, Attempts, Receipts, and Artifacts"
subtitle: "How is durable evidence appended and resolved safely?"
toc-depth: 2
---

**Status:** `CONVERGING` implementation design.

## Bind one workspace to one Plan and runtime

A V1 workspace is a relocatable directory with one sealed Plan and numerical
runtime binding plus append-only request attempts:

```text
workspace.json
plan.json
requests/<request-sha256>/
  request.json
  attempts/000001/
    attempt.json
    logs/
    artifacts/result.zarr/
    result.json
    receipt.json
```

The workspace location is not part of computational request identity. It
selects the evidence store in which that request must be found; relocating the
whole verified workspace does not rename the request. All stored paths are
relative to the workspace. `receipt.json` is written last and only after Python
verifies the attempt outcome. It seals success, typed failure, or interruption;
only a verified success receipt can materialize a Result. A temporary staging
directory is never a successful Result.

V1 uses one writer lock per workspace; different workspaces may run in
parallel. This deliberately simple ceiling avoids two processes selecting the
same next attempt number or sealing competing successes. Per-request locking
is considered only if measured same-workspace throughput requires it.

## Reuse success and append failure history

The request directory is derived from canonical request identity. If one
attempt contains a complete verified success, the terminal operation returns
it. Otherwise a new call appends the next immutable attempt. Failed and
interrupted attempts remain visible to `inventory()` and cannot be overwritten.

A verified `HBBatchResult` is successful request evidence even when every case
contains a numerical `HBCaseFailure`; repeating it reuses the batch. Only a
request-level failure or interruption is retryable.

`resolve()` acquires no execution slot. It recomputes the request identity,
finds the verified success, and validates Plan, runtime, receipt, manifest, and
artifact hashes. Missing or corrupt evidence is an error; it never falls back
to another attempt or request.

## Store arrays without pickling

Scalar metadata, schemas, failures, and receipts use canonical JSON. Large real
arrays use Zarr V2 chunks; complex arrays use paired Float64 real/imag arrays
with one typed manifest. V1 starts with uncompressed chunks so another language
can implement the format without a codec dependency. The OGC-endorsed
[Zarr V2 standard](https://www.ogc.org/standards/zarr-storage-specification/)
defines JSON metadata and optionally compressed binary chunks for
multidimensional arrays.

Chunk shape, array order, dtype, axes, units, coordinate IDs, and real/imag
pairing are manifest authority. A Python Result may load chunks lazily, but
must reconstruct the declared NumPy/Pint surface before returning it.
